data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The criticism mechanism fails to retire rivals because the Dung grounded extension attack pass does not enforce coverage debt as a degradation trigger, leading to unbounded rivalry from variators. Introducing a criterion-level forced choice would bound rivalry. A sandboxed_python_v1 simulation testing the growth of unretired positions under batched criticism with versus without forced-choice degradation\u2014alongside Wikipedia research on Dung's argumentation frameworks and peer review\u2014would discriminate these predictions.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The grounded extension might already be sufficient if the issue is merely insufficient attack density rather than the extension algorithm itself.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"Variators could be tuned to reduce novelty instead of changing the criticism mechanism.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"Coverage debt may not monotonically correlate with retirement if defenders can effectively resolve warrants.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Variators generate inequivalent survivors (s(a) > 0) independently of strict attack coverage, meaning many positions survive simply because they are unattacked. The grounded extension settles on a skeptical state but does not actively degrade or retire high-coverage-debt nodes. By enforcing a forced-choice degradation criterion tied to coverage debt, the survival probability of un-attacked or poorly-defended nodes is directly lowered, actively retiring positions rather than allowing them to coexist. This can be tested in a sandboxed Python simulation by comparing rivalry size over time under random batched criticism versus forced-choice degradation. Wikipedia fetches on Dung's frameworks and peer review processes would provide theoretical bounds for the simulation's parameters.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
